body:
# Independent audit of the normal-preserving boundary coupling

**Result: PASS.** I independently read every section of
`candidate 7278f286325c46c7`, including
the finite separation argument, both compact approximation
constructions, the parameter-preserving lifting argument, the
measurable supporting-plane selector, and the automatic preservation
of normals for actual fibers. I found no mathematical gap requiring
a change to the proof source.

This is an audit of the stated geometric transport theorem. It does
not audit existence of a variational minimum or its stress certificate;
those are separate hypotheses in the source. It also does not assert
gamma_d/h(P) for arbitrary finite bases, which is false. Any further
OC implication must retain the lattice-complete parity-budget setting
described in `historical context (not an accepted premise)`.

## 1. Finite convex order and separation

The distance to the target convex hull is an admissible finite
continuous convex test. Because it is nonnegative and vanishes on
every target atom, each positive source atom lies in that hull.
Consequently the row-mass and row-barycenter polytope is nonempty;
bounded row masses also make it compact. Its column-sum image is
compact and convex, so strict separation from an infeasible target
column vector gives the displayed strict inequality with its
correct orientation.

The lower convex envelope of the finitely many values b_j is the
rowwise minimum in that separation. Its domain is the compact
polytope conv{y_j}. The vertical-ray epigraph is a polyhedron; its
lower nonvertical facets give finitely many affine functions whose
maximum agrees with the lower envelope on the entire domain,
including boundary faces. There cannot be a domain point with no
nonvertical active lower constraint, since that would allow its
height to decrease without bound. Extending those affine functions
from the affine span and taking their finite maximum is therefore
a genuine finite continuous convex extension. The dimension-zero
constant case is explicitly covered.

Each target value satisfies f(y_j)<=b_j, and independent rowwise
minimization gives precisely sum_i m_i f(x_i). Convex order then
contradicts the strict separator. No unproved infinite-dimensional
transport theorem is concealed in this finite step.

## 2. The two grid approximations have the correct order

Contracting a source cell to its conditional barycenter gives
nu_delta<=cx nu by Jensen. Splitting a target point among its cube
vertices with multilinear weights gives mu<=cx mu_delta^+, again
by Jensen. Both constructions preserve total mass and first
moments. Using opposite directions here is essential and the
source has them correctly.

The half-open convention removes grid-boundary ambiguity, and
bounded support leaves finitely many occupied cells. Conditional
barycenters and cube vertices stay within a common fixed compact
box. The maximum displacement is at most sqrt(k)delta, which
proves the asserted weak convergence without any regularity of
the measures or absence of boundary atoms.

Weak compactness of finite measures of fixed mass on the compact
product box supplies a subsequential coupling limit. The marginal
identities and all continuous row-moment tests pass to this limit.
For each physical coordinate, the expression

    B -> integral_(B times Y) (y_i-x_i) dpi

is a finite signed Borel measure. It integrates every continuous
function to zero, so uniqueness of finite measures on a compact
space makes it zero. This proves the extension to every bounded
Borel test, rather than assuming such tests pass through weak
convergence directly.

## 3. Parameter localization and preservation

For each fixed affine or convex physical test, integration against
eta-nu produces a finite signed measure on the compact parameter
space. The continuous-test assumptions imply, respectively, that
this measure is zero or nonnegative. Therefore restriction to
every Borel parameter cell preserves equal mass and physical
convex order. There is no parameter-dependent exceptional set
introduced by this argument.

Finite Borel partitions of arbitrarily small diameter exist on
every compact metric parameter space. A physical coupling can be
chosen separately in each of their finitely many cells. Since both
measures are concentrated on the same Borel normal graph, lifting
by the normal map gives the required bundle marginals. The
lifted moment identity follows from the already proved bounded-
Borel version of the physical identity, using the test
f(n(x),x). No continuity of the normal map is improperly used at
this lifting step.

The lifted measures are concentrated on the fixed compact relation
N times N. In the weak limit, the continuous parameter-distance
function has integral zero because its previous integrals were
at most delta times the total mass. Thus the two parameters agree
almost everywhere. Continuous row moments then pass to the limit,
and the same signed-measure argument extends them to bounded
Borel tests. Fixed marginals ensure that possible irregular graph
points in the compact closure retain zero marginal mass.

This construction avoids a measurable choice of couplings indexed
by individual normals; only finitely many choices are made before
each compact limit.

## 4. Boundary measures and normal measurability

For finitely many compact positive-dimensional convex fibers,
the stated normal relation is compact: support functions are
continuous in the unit normal, and the exposed-face equality is
closed. Boundary area is finite; in d=1 it is the counting measure
on the two distinct endpoints.

For d>=2, the standard Lipschitz-chart and differentiability
description of a convex boundary makes nonregular points surface-
null. The normal is Borel on the regular part. An additional direct
description verifies the latter point: the compact unit-normal
multifunction has closed graph, its singleton locus is Borel, and
on that locus uniqueness plus compactness makes the normal map
continuous relative to the regular locus. Extending it arbitrarily
on the null complement supplies the common Borel map needed in
Section 3. Absolute continuity nu<<eta preserves that null set.

The base label p is part of the physical coordinate, so different
fibers never become identified during this construction. The
resulting row identities retain both the base coordinate and every
continuous coordinate. Conditional probabilities are optional:
the displayed bounded-Borel identities already encode all needed
row assertions.

## 5. Supporting-plane selector for actual fibers

For C=conv(union_p {p} times K_p), its section support at z is

    max_{alpha>=0, sum alpha=1, sum alpha p=z}
                                      sum alpha_p h_p(u).

This is the exact finite convex-hull formula. At each listed p,
actual-section compatibility says its value is h_p(u). This
equality is the indispensable geometric hypothesis; it is not
valid for an arbitrary family whose own section is enlarged by
taking the joint convex hull.

The affine-majorant dual is feasible and has finite attained
optimum h_p(u). The usual finite linear-programming duality
applies, including when p lies on the boundary of the base hull.
After restricting affine functions to E=aff(P), its feasible
polyhedron has no lineality: an affine function vanishing at every
point of P vanishes on E. A nonempty optimal face of this pointed
polyhedron therefore contains a vertex. At a vertex, r+1 active
evaluation constraints have independent rows; otherwise a small
two-sided coefficient variation would preserve feasibility and
contradict extremality. These rows correspond exactly to r+1
affinely independent base points.

There are finitely many such subsets. Each associated affine
interpolant depends continuously on u, because the base evaluation
matrix is fixed and invertible and every h_q(u) is continuous.
Its feasibility and touching conditions are closed conditions
in u. Choosing the first feasible touching interpolant is therefore
Borel. All candidate coefficients are bounded on the compact
normal sphere, so the selected slopes are uniformly bounded.
The affine-rank-zero case is correctly treated separately.

One may represent the slope in the direction space of E and
extend it by zero on its orthogonal complement; no full base rank
or lattice-changing coordinate transformation is required.

## 6. Automatic preservation of the continuous normal

At a regular input (p,x), the selected affine majorant gives an
ambient supporting inequality through that point. Its nonnegative
output gap is exactly

    h_p(u)+s(u,p).(q-p)-u.y
      =s(u,p).(q-p)-u.(y-x).

Both coefficients are bounded Borel functions of the input. The
full physical row-barycenter identities therefore force its
integral to vanish, also after restriction to any input set.
Since the gap is nonnegative, it is zero almost everywhere.

The two inequalities u.y<=h_q(u)<=l_(u,p)(q) can then both be
equalities only if u.y=h_q(u). Thus u is an outer normal at the
output point. The target measure is concentrated on regular
boundary points, where the unit outer normal is unique. This
forces equality of input and output normals. The conclusion holds
for every martingale coupling with these physical marginals, not
only for a specially selected one.

Conversely, a normal-preserving row-barycenter coupling gives the
localized affine identities and convex inequalities by rowwise
Jensen and preservation of the normal parameter. Compact-space
conditional measures, if used for this description, are legitimate;
the existence argument itself did not need their measurable
selection.

## Scope conclusion

All zero-mass, affine-rank-zero, d=1, grid-boundary, boundary-atom,
and nonregular-boundary cases required by this transport theorem
are handled. No selected mixed-integer center or mixed volume
transport is inferred. Its geometric conclusion applies to any
finite actual fiber family with the stated convex-order data,
but the numerical OC implication cannot be extended to arbitrary
finite sampling bases. The corrected lattice-complete parity
budget remains necessary for that separate task.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
